info.name: Cortex API
info.description:
cortex-api (Spring Boot backend for Cortex) — Auth, Notes CRUD, Full-text Search, and the Sync Engine, including self-contained, runnable demos of the sync engine's evolution (spec §5):
- Stage 2: naive whole-note LWW silently destroying data (historical — the push request shape has changed twice since, so this folder no longer runs against the current API; kept as a record of the original bug).
- Stage 3/4: field-level LWW with optimistic-concurrency conflict detection. Each field's `...BaseUpdatedAt` is a version token, not a clock timestamp — a client reports what it last saw for that field before editing it. If the field's current stored token no longer matches, someone else changed it since — that's a genuine CONFLICT (the edit is preserved as a separate, visible duplicate note, never silently discarded), not just "my clock says I'm later."

Before using this collection:
1. The app must be running locally on the `baseUrl` below (default `http://localhost:8080`) — Postgres reachable, Redis reachable (auto-started by `spring-boot-docker-compose`), and `JWT_SECRET` exported in the shell that launches the app.
2. Run **Auth > Register** first to populate the `accessToken`/`refreshToken` collection variables used by every other folder — except the **Stage 2** and **Stage 3/4** demo folders, which each register their own user and are fully self-contained.

request.description: Registers a fresh user (unique email generated per run) and saves the returned access/refresh tokens as collection variables, used by every other request via the collection-level Bearer auth.
Re-uses the email from the last Register call (edit the body to log in as a different account).

exec: pm.test('Refresh token was rotated (different from the one we sent)', function () {

request.description: Rotates the refresh token. Run this twice in a row with the same stored token to see reuse-detection kick in (second call gets a 401, INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN).

List response items never include `body` — proof is in the query itself, not just the DTO shape. Paste the `nextCursor` from a response into the disabled `cursor` param (and enable it) to get the next page.

Response includes `titleUpdatedAt`/`bodyUpdatedAt` (saved as `noteTitleBase`/`noteBodyBase`) — the per-field version tokens a real sync client must read before constructing its next `/sync/push` (see the Sync folder), and `conflictOf`/`conflictField`, populated only on a note that was created as someone's rejected-conflict copy.
Returns 204 with no body. Redis cache entry for this note is evicted as part of the same request.
Full-text search, ranked by relevance (title matches weighted above body matches). Cursor-paginated the same way as List Notes.

query.description: ISO-8601 instant. Omit for a first-time sync (returns everything). Use the `nextSince` from a previous pull response as the `since` for the next one (it deliberately overlaps the last window, so a note may arrive twice; apply idempotently) — never the client's own clock.

request.description: Each returned note includes `titleUpdatedAt`/`bodyUpdatedAt` — a real client stores these locally per note as its 'base', and echoes them back unchanged on its next push for any field it didn't edit.

Optimistic-concurrency field-level sync. Each field is accepted only if its `...BaseUpdatedAt` exactly matches the note's CURRENT stored value for that field — i.e. nothing changed underneath you since you last knew about this field. If it doesn't match: ACCEPTED becomes either REJECTED_STALE (your content already matches what's stored — nothing lost) or CONFLICT (your content differs — a duplicate note is created holding your version, and `conflictNoteId` in the response points to it). Run **Notes > Get Note** first to refresh `{{noteTitleBase}}`/`{{noteBodyBase}}` to the current values. Uses `{{noteId}}` from the Notes folder by default; for an ID that doesn't exist yet for this user, this creates it (client-generated ID preserved).

item.name: Stage 2 — Naive Whole-Note LWW (historical, no longer runs)
item.description: HISTORICAL — kept as a record of the original bug, not runnable against the current API. This folder's requests use the very first push contract (`clientUpdatedAt`); the request shape has since changed twice (field-level timestamps in stage 3, then base-matching in stage 4). See the **Stage 3/4** folder for the current, runnable version of this same concurrent-edit scenario.

item.name: 2. Push using the ORIGINAL (now-defunct) clientUpdatedAt contract — expect 400

request.description: This is the ORIGINAL stage-2 push shape. `NotePushItem` no longer has a `clientUpdatedAt` field (it now requires `titleBaseUpdatedAt`/`bodyBaseUpdatedAt`), so this request fails validation — proof, by itself, that the naive whole-note design has been fully replaced, not patched around.

item.name: Stage 3/4 — Field-Level LWW + Conflict Surfacing
item.description:
Three scenarios, run in order. Each is self-contained (registers its own user).

**A (0-4): different fields, concurrently edited.** Device A edits only the title, Device B only the body — offline, unaware of each other, both correctly echo back their unedited field's BASE token. Both edits survive: this is what field-level LWW alone (stage 3) already fixes.

**B (5-8): the SAME field, concurrently edited — the case stage 3 alone could NOT fix.** Device A edits the title, based on the shared original. Device B ALSO edits the title, based on that SAME original base — never having seen Device A's edit. Because Device B's base no longer matches what's actually stored (Device A's edit already landed), this is now correctly detected as a genuine CONFLICT: Device A's edit is preserved untouched, and Device B's edit survives too — as a separate, fully visible duplicate note — instead of one silently overwriting the other.

**C (9-10): the noop case — proves the design doesn't spawn junk duplicates.** A push whose base is stale AND whose content already matches what's stored (e.g. a retried request) is correctly just REJECTED_STALE, not CONFLICT — no duplicate note is created for something that changed nothing.

exec: pm.test('bodyOutcome is ACCEPTED (base matches — A honestly echoed the unedited field)', function () { pm.expect(r.bodyOutcome).to.eql('ACCEPTED'); });

request.description: Device B's title is unchanged from the ORIGINAL — it matches what device B last saw, but not what's currently stored (A already changed it). Since B's title content equals the pre-A-edit original and NOT the current stored title, this correctly resolves as REJECTED_STALE, not CONFLICT — B isn't asserting a conflicting edit, it's just out of date on a field it never touched.

pm.test('Device B\'s body edit survived', function () { pm.expect(jsonData.data.body).to.include('Action items'); });

request.description: THIS is the case naive whole-note LWW (stage 2) AND field-level-LWW-without-conflict-detection would both get wrong: Device B's title genuinely differs from what's stored, and its base is stale. Base-matching alone (used for accept/reject) can't tell 'this is a deliberate overwrite' from 'this is an independent edit that never saw A's change' — so instead of picking a winner, this is surfaced as a CONFLICT and BOTH versions are kept.

request.description: Stale base (the original, pre-A-edit one) but the title content ('Paris trip') exactly matches what's currently stored — e.g. a client retrying a push it never got a response for. Correctly resolves as REJECTED_STALE, not CONFLICT: nothing would be gained by creating a duplicate here.
